title: Electric and Magnetic Fields
learning_goal: Identify and describe electric and magnetic forces and fields and connect them to everyday devices.

stages.title: 1. Fields describe forces at a distance
stages.content: Electric and magnetic fields describe regions where charges or magnets can experience forces without direct contact. Field direction shows the direction a positive test charge or north magnetic pole would tend to move.

stages.title: 2. Electric fields
stages.content: Electric fields are produced by electric charges. Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges. Stronger fields are represented by more closely spaced field lines.

stages.title: 3. Magnetic fields
stages.content: Magnetic fields are produced by magnets and moving electric charges. Outside a bar magnet, field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole.

stages.title: 4. Everyday applications
stages.content: Motors use magnetic forces on current-carrying wires. Generators use changing magnetic fields to produce electric current. Transformers use changing magnetic fields to transfer electrical energy between coils.

stages.title: 5. Guided practice
stages.prompt: A wire carrying current is placed in a magnetic field and experiences a force. What does this show about electricity and magnetism?
stages.hint: Think about what produces magnetic fields and what can experience magnetic forces.
stages.alternate_explanation: Moving charges create magnetic effects, so a current-carrying wire can interact with an external magnetic field.
stages.answer: Electric current and magnetic fields interact to produce force.

stages.title: 6. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, identify electric and magnetic fields, describe field direction, compare electric and magnetic interactions, and explain how motors, generators, and transformers use those interactions.

concept_cards.title: What does the direction of an electric field arrow mean?
concept_cards.content: A field describes force per unit positive test charge. Particle velocity need not point along its force.

concept_cards.content: Magnetic force on a point charge is qv × B; zero velocity makes this magnetic contribution zero.
